title: Below-average precipitation continuation
description: The onset of a precipitation deficit serves as a key early-warning trigger in Afghanistan’s drought cycle, as sustained below-average rainfall reduces soil moisture, delays snow accumulation, and weakens river and groundwater recharge. According to the World Meteorological Organization and FEWS NET, such early deficits rapidly translate into water shortages that undermine winter crop growth and pasture regeneration, threatening food and income sources for farming and herding households. title: Nationwide hartal calls or election boycott by major political parties
description: If major political parties, particularly the BNP or allied opposition groups formally announce nationwide hartals or an election boycott, the likelihood of widespread political violence would increase sharply. Such announcements would likely prompt mass mobilization, transport blockades, and confrontations between party supporters, security forces, and rival groups. Based on patterns from previous election cycles, hartal calls are often followed by pre-emptive security deployments, arrests of opposition activists, and the use of force to keep transport routes and economic hubs open. A boycott would also undermine the perceived legitimacy of the electoral process, increasing incentives for disruptive or violent actions both before and during polling, particularly in urban centres. title: Breackdown of peace talks
description: Concerns are growing over the potential breakdown of peace negotiations between the Colombian Government and the Gaitanist Self-Defense Forces of Colombia (EGC), the largest and most influential non-state armed group in the country. According to official estimates, the EGC increased its membership by 95% between 2018 and 2024, reaching around 7,000 members—including 2,499 combatants and 4,563 support network members—by mid-2024. The group has expanded its territorial control in several departments, particularly Chocó, Magdalena Medio, southern Bolívar, and the Caribbean coast, where it has consolidated strategic corridors linked to illicit economies. Between 2023 and 2024, its armed capacity in southern Bolívar alone grew by 23%, highlighting a clear strengthening trend amid ongoing peace talks. This continued military expansion and territorial consolidation raise doubts about the EGC’s genuine willingness to engage in disarmament or comply with potential peace accords. A collapse of the peace process could intensify clashes with other armed actors, notably the ELN and FARC-EP dissident factions, leading to further mass displacement, confinement, targeted killings, and restrictions on humanitarian access. title: Prolonged Drought and Heatwaves
description: Iran’s worsening water crisis is being driven by prolonged drought and intensifying heatwaves, which have sharply reduced rainfall, surface water, and groundwater reserves. Between October 2024 and March 2025, precipitation declined by 41% below long-term averages and 21% compared to the previous year, severely limiting inflows into dams and reservoirs. The deficit now affects 30 of 31 provinces, with the harshest shortfalls recorded in Hormozgan (–75.9%), Sistan-Baluchestan (–75.4%), and East Azerbaijan (–60%). Record-breaking heat has accelerated evaporation, compounding the depletion of already scarce supplies. In Tehran, key reservoirs, Latian, Lar, Mamloo, and Amir Kabir, have dropped to just 5–12% capacity, with the Lar dam nearly empty, threatening water security and essential urban services. The combined effects of persistent drought, extreme heat, and excessive groundwater extraction have disrupted Iran’s hydrological balance, leading to land subsidence, reduced agricultural output, and growing food insecurity. These climatic pressures are central triggers of Iran’s water crisis, exacerbating structural weaknesses in governance, infrastructure, and livelihoods. title: Climate Change Amplification
description: Climate change is a major amplifier of Iran’s water crisis, intensifying droughts, heatwaves, and rainfall variability across much of the country. Rising temperatures have accelerated evaporation and reduced snowpack in key mountain ranges, diminishing surface runoff that feeds rivers and reservoirs. Over the past two decades, Iran’s average temperature has increased by more than 1.5°C, with extreme heat events becoming longer and more frequent. This climatic shift has disrupted traditional rainfall cycles, concentrating precipitation into shorter, more intense bursts that fail to replenish groundwater or sustain agriculture. As a result, 30 of 31 provinces now face chronic water stress, with southern and central regions, such as Khuzestan, Yazd, and Sistan-Baluchestan, experiencing the most severe shortages. Higher temperatures also drive surging demand for irrigation and domestic consumption, compounding existing overuse of groundwater and depletion of reservoirs. The resulting imbalance has caused widespread subsidence, declining crop yields, and rural displacement. title: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions
description: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions: During El Niño events, large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts suppress moisture transport into southern Africa, reducing rainfall during the main cropping season. In southern and central Mozambique, this often results in prolonged dry spells, erratic rainfall distribution, and early cessation of rains rather than a complete absence of precipitation. At the same time, above-average temperatures increase evapotranspiration rates, accelerating the loss of soil moisture and surface water. This combination reduces water availability for domestic consumption, crops and livestock, heightens the risk of pasture degradation, and can lead to reduced agricultural yields or crop failure, particularly for rainfed smallholder farmers. title: Security Vacuum and Porous Borders
description: Capitalising on weak cross-border collaboration, the group/Lakurawa exploited challenging terrains to infiltrate remote areas in northwestern states and disseminate its ideology. Moreover, the already strained relations between Nigeria and Niger exacerbated by Niger’s July 2023 coup disrupted joint military operations, thereby enabling the Lakurawa group to broaden its influence further. The porous borders between northwest Nigeria and its neighbouring countries, along with limited border control, have significantly contributed to the prevailing insecurity in affected communities. This vulnerability is compounded by the lack of a strong security presence in many remote areas. Non-state armed groups like Lakurawa take advantage of these weaknesses; they do not recognise established borders or state authority but instead strive to carve out their own mini-states, where they govern, levy taxes, and impose their rules and ideology. title: Below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures
description: El Niño typically suppresses rainfall across the Philippines while also contributing to above-average temperatures. During the monsoon season, it also contributes to irregular rainfall distribution, characterized by intermittent dry spells and uneven precipitation. Reduced or unheavenly distributed rainfall, combined with high temperatures, increases evapotranspiration, accelerating the depletion of soil moisture, while reduced precipitation affect surface and groundwater reserves. This can significantly reduce water availability for domestic consumption, irrigation, and livestock, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces. Prolonged heat and moisture stress can also damage crops during critical growth stages, reduce agricultural productivity, and increase heat-related health risks, especially among affected rural households and outdoor workers.
